agent.name: Embedded Project Idea Scoping Agent
agent.context: Embedded Engineering and Gen AI Summer School for third-year Computer Science students
agent.purpose: Convert a vague embedded project idea into a structured scoping brief for requirements engineering

fixed_platform.pin_policy: Use generic capabilities unless exact pins are provided
fixed_platform.logic_level_policy: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise

project.name: FRDM-MCXA153 Walkie Talkie Prototype
project.short_summary: A push-to-talk embedded audio communication prototype built around the mandatory NXP FRDM-MCXA153 board, with scope levels from local audio loopback to short-range digital voice messaging using external audio and communication modules.
project.main_objective: Demonstrate a handheld-style push-to-talk communication device using the FRDM-MCXA153 as the control, audio processing, and user-interface platform.
project.operating_environment: Indoor lab or classroom environment with short communication distances and controlled power conditions.
project.main_behavior: The user presses a push-to-talk control, speaks into a microphone, and the device captures audio, indicates transmit or receive state, and either plays audio locally or exchanges audio data with a paired unit depending on the selected scope.
inputs: Microphone signal through a suitable 3.3 V-compatible audio front end or digital microphone module
Optional received data from a communication module
outputs: Speaker or headphones through a suitable low-power audio amplifier or DAC/audio output module
Optional small display for channel, battery, and state
interaction_flow: Device initializes audio input, audio output, user controls, and optional communication module.
User selects a channel or default operating mode if implemented.
Device indicates transmit mode and captures microphone audio.
In the core version, captured audio is used for local test playback or level indication.
In the recommended version, audio is packetized or sampled and sent to a paired device over an external communication module.
Receiving device indicates receive mode and plays the received audio through the audio output path.
out_of_scope: Replacing the FRDM-MCXA153 with another main controller board
Commercial radio certification or long-range radio product design
Guaranteed compatibility with 5 V audio or radio modules without level shifting verification

problem_space.purpose: Explore embedded audio capture, simple real-time behavior, user interaction, and short-range communication in a student-friendly project.
problem_space.physical_process_monitored_or_controlled: Human speech sound pressure is converted to an electrical or digital audio signal, processed by the MCU, and converted back to audible sound locally or on a paired device.
success_criteria: A user can clearly enter transmit mode using a push-to-talk control.
The system provides visible feedback for idle, transmit, receive, and error states.
The core version can capture audio or audio level data reliably enough for demonstration.
The recommended version can send intelligible short voice snippets or low-rate audio between two prototypes in a controlled lab setting.
The design uses 3.3 V-compatible interfaces or explicitly documented level shifting and power isolation.
known_constraints: The NXP FRDM-MCXA153 board and NXP MCXA153 MCU are mandatory.
Exact pins are not specified and must be chosen later from generic GPIO, ADC, I2C, SPI, UART, PWM, or USB capabilities.
Audio and radio modules must be verified for 3.3 V logic compatibility.
Real-time audio streaming may be constrained by MCU resources, communication bandwidth, buffering, and latency.
unknown_constraints: Whether the final prototype requires one board only, two boards, or communication with a phone or PC.
Required range, audio quality, and acceptable latency.
Available microphone, speaker, amplifier, and radio modules in the lab kit.

core_student_version.description: Single-board push-to-talk audio trainer: the FRDM-MCXA153 reads a push-to-talk button, samples a microphone or audio module, shows audio level and state with LEDs or serial output, and optionally plays back short recorded snippets through a simple audio output path.
expected_features: Audio level meter using LEDs or serial logs
Optional local playback through a low-power speaker or headphone output module
Simple state machine for idle, record, playback, and error states
core_student_version.why_it_is_suitable: It teaches GPIO, basic audio sampling, buffering, timing, state machines, and debugging without requiring a working radio link in the first milestone.

recommended_summer_school_version.description: Two-board short-range digital walkie-talkie demonstrator: each FRDM-MCXA153 unit has push-to-talk control, microphone input, speaker output, status indicators, and an external 3.3 V-compatible communication module for half-duplex audio packet exchange.
expected_features: Packet buffering with sequence numbers or simple framing
Serial debug view for packet counts, dropped packets, and state transitions
Basic channel or device pairing concept
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_interesting: It behaves like a recognizable walkie-talkie while exposing students to embedded audio, communication protocols, buffering, and human-facing interaction design.
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_still_feasible: The feature set can be reduced to low audio quality or short voice snippets if real-time streaming proves too demanding, while still preserving the core walkie-talkie behavior.

advanced_extension.description: Enhanced digital voice communicator with optional compression, recorded voice messages, display UI, battery monitoring, logging, and GenAI-assisted test and protocol documentation.
advanced_features: Simple audio compression or companding experiment
Small display showing channel, state, signal quality, and battery estimate
Packet loss statistics and diagnostic logging
Optional PC-side visualization of audio levels and packet timing
Optional edge AI concept such as wake-word-free speech activity classification or noise classification if a suitable model and memory budget are confirmed
extra_components: 3.3 V-compatible digital microphone or microphone front-end module
Low-power audio amplifier and small speaker
Battery holder or regulated power module with protection
Optional external memory module if long recordings are required
technical_challenges: Maintaining stable sampling and playback timing
Managing latency and buffering over a limited-bandwidth link
Avoiding audio clipping, noise, and feedback
Fitting advanced audio or AI features into available memory and CPU budget
Designing a clear half-duplex protocol and user experience
risk_controls: Begin with local loopback before enabling wireless communication.
Use low sample rates and short buffers for early milestones.
Prefer certified low-power communication modules instead of custom RF transmitter design.
Verify 3.3 V logic compatibility before connecting modules.
Use an external amplifier designed for the selected speaker rather than driving a speaker directly from MCU pins.

main_board.name: NXP FRDM-MCXA153
main_board.reasoning: Mandatory board for all summer school projects

sensors.name: Microphone module or audio front end
sensors.purpose: Capture speech audio from the user.
sensors.likely_interface: ADC-capable input for analog microphone front end, or I2S/SPI/PDM-like digital audio interface if supported by selected hardware and SDK configuration
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: Must be verified as 3.3 V-compatible; analog microphone front ends may require biasing, filtering, and gain.
risks: Unconfirmed digital audio interface support until hardware and SDK configuration are selected

sensors.name: Optional battery voltage monitor
sensors.purpose: Estimate supply or battery level for portable operation.
sensors.likely_interface: ADC-capable input through a safe voltage divider
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: Divider must keep the ADC input within the FRDM-MCXA153 safe input range.
risks: Incorrect divider may exceed input voltage limits
Battery-powered designs require protection and charging considerations

actuators_outputs.name: Low-power audio amplifier and speaker or headphone output module
actuators_outputs.likely_interface: PWM-capable output with filtering, DAC/audio-capable output if available, I2S/SPI audio output module if selected, or external amplifier input
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Do not drive a speaker directly from MCU pins; amplifier power and logic levels must be verified.
risks: Speaker current exceeds MCU pin capability
5 V amplifier modules may require level shifting

actuators_outputs.name: Status LEDs
actuators_outputs.purpose: Indicate idle, transmit, receive, pairing, recording, playback, or error state.
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Use appropriate current limiting and respect board I/O limits.
risks: Incorrect resistor selection can exceed safe current

user_inputs.name: Push-to-talk button
user_inputs.likely_interface: GPIO-capable pin with pull-up or pull-down configuration
user_inputs.notes: Debouncing should be handled in software or hardware.

user_inputs.name: Optional channel or volume buttons
user_inputs.purpose: Change channel, volume, or operating mode.
user_inputs.likely_interface: GPIO-capable pins, ADC resistor ladder, or existing board-compatible input method
user_inputs.notes: Exact input method should follow available lab components.

display_ui.name: LED-only interface
display_ui.purpose: Provide minimal visible status for core demonstration.
display_ui.notes: Sufficient for first milestone and debugging.

display_ui.name: Optional small display
display_ui.purpose: Show channel, transmit/receive state, packet quality, and battery status.
display_ui.notes: Use a 3.3 V-compatible display module or provide level shifting if required.

communication_debug.name: USB serial debug connection
communication_debug.purpose: Log state transitions, audio buffer statistics, packet counts, and errors during development.
communication_debug.likely_interface: USB interface or board-supported serial debug interface
communication_debug.notes: Useful for development and demo diagnostics.

communication_debug.name: External short-range wireless module
communication_debug.purpose: Exchange audio packets or voice snippets between two devices.
communication_debug.likely_interface: SPI-capable pins, UART-capable pins, or I2C-capable pins depending on selected module
communication_debug.notes: Prefer a 3.3 V-compatible low-power module with clear documentation and legal operation in the local lab environment.

power_source.recommended_power: USB power for core and recommended lab demonstrations; optional regulated battery power only after current draw and protection needs are verified.
power_source.notes: Audio amplifiers, displays, and wireless modules may add current draw beyond a minimal board-only project.
risks: Battery operation introduces charging, protection, and voltage regulation concerns.
External modules may require more current than the board headers should provide.
Grounding and noise from the audio amplifier may affect microphone quality.

optional_advanced_components.name: Certified low-power wireless transceiver module
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Provide the communication link for real walkie-talkie behavior.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_include: Enables a convincing two-device demonstration without designing RF circuitry from scratch.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Adds protocol, bandwidth, latency, power, and regulatory considerations.

optional_advanced_components.name: Audio codec or digital audio module
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Improve audio input and output quality compared with simple ADC/PWM experiments.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_include: Can simplify analog audio quality problems and enable cleaner playback.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: May require more complex interface configuration and driver work.

optional_advanced_components.name: Small display module
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Provide a richer user interface for channel and diagnostics.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_include: Improves demo clarity and user feedback.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Consumes time and I/O bandwidth that may be better spent on audio and communication first.
risks: Display update timing interfering with audio if poorly scheduled

software_context.recommended_development_environment: NXP-supported embedded C development environment for the FRDM-MCXA153, selected by the course staff or project template.
recommended_sdk_or_libraries: NXP MCUXpresso SDK components appropriate for the FRDM-MCXA153 board
Board support and startup files from the provided course template
Peripheral drivers selected after confirming the final microphone, audio output, display, and communication modules
Optional lightweight ring buffer or packet framing utilities implemented or reviewed by students
software_context.suggested_starting_point: Start from a minimal FRDM-MCXA153 project that blinks an LED and reads a button, then add microphone sampling or audio level measurement, then local buffering/playback, and only then add the wireless link.
debugging_interfaces: Optional PC-side serial monitor or plotting tool

constraints.voltage: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise
constraints.power: Use USB power for early prototypes; verify external module and audio amplifier current requirements before battery operation.
constraints.timing: Audio capture, playback, and packet transfer require predictable timing, buffering, and latency control.
constraints.memory: Audio buffers, recorded snippets, packet queues, and any advanced processing must fit within the available MCU memory.
constraints.safety: Avoid direct speaker drive from MCU pins, unsafe batteries, high-power RF, or unverified 5 V connections.
constraints.privacy_security: Voice audio may contain personal data; demos should avoid recording or transmitting sensitive speech and should document whether audio is stored.

complexity.reason: A walkie-talkie is a strong educational project but real-time audio plus wireless communication can become difficult; a staged scope with local audio first and wireless second keeps it achievable.

facts_provided_by_user: The project idea is a walkie talkie.
The project must use the NXP FRDM-MCXA153 board.
The output JSON path is project_scoping_brief.json.
The project should include a core student version, a recommended version, and an advanced extension.
Exact pins and SDK APIs must not be invented.

assumptions.assumption: The prototype is intended for a lab demonstration rather than a certified consumer radio product.
assumptions.reason: The input only says walkie talkie, and certification or long-range RF design would be outside a normal student embedded prototype.

assumptions.assumption: Two FRDM-MCXA153-based devices may be available for the recommended version.
assumptions.reason: A true walkie-talkie demonstration normally requires two endpoints, but the user did not specify the number of boards.

assumptions.assumption: Short-range low-power digital communication modules are acceptable for the recommended version.
assumptions.reason: The FRDM-MCXA153 should remain the main board, while an external communication module is a realistic way to avoid unsafe or impractical RF design.

assumptions.assumption: Low audio quality is acceptable for early milestones.
assumptions.reason: Reduced sample rates and short buffers make the project more achievable for students.

assumptions.assumption: USB-powered operation is acceptable for the first prototype.
assumptions.reason: Battery operation adds power management and safety concerns that are not required to demonstrate core embedded behavior.

open_questions.question: Should the recommended prototype use one device with local loopback, two FRDM-MCXA153 devices, or one FRDM-MCXA153 device communicating with a PC or phone?
open_questions.why_it_matters: This determines the communication architecture, hardware quantity, and demonstration plan.

open_questions.question: What communication module or technology is available in the course lab kit?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Wireless bandwidth, latency, interface type, power needs, and driver effort depend heavily on the selected module.

open_questions.question: Is real-time voice streaming required, or are short recorded voice messages acceptable?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Store-and-forward snippets are much easier than continuous low-latency audio streaming.

open_questions.question: What audio quality is considered acceptable for the demo?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Sample rate, buffer size, amplifier choice, and communication bandwidth depend on this requirement.

open_questions.question: Must the final prototype be battery powered?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Battery operation affects power budgeting, enclosure design, safety controls, and hardware selection.

open_questions.question: Which microphone, speaker, amplifier, and display modules are physically available?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Requirements should be grounded in real components and their voltage/interface limitations.

technical: Real-time voice streaming may exceed the practical bandwidth or timing budget of the selected communication module.
Audio input and output quality may be poor without suitable amplification, filtering, and buffering.
Two-device synchronization and half-duplex state handling can introduce hard-to-debug edge cases.
External module driver integration may consume more time than expected.
safety: Speakers and amplifiers must not be powered directly from MCU pins.
Battery operation requires protection, regulation, and current budgeting.
High-volume audio output should be avoided, especially with headphones.
voltage_power: Some common audio, display, or radio breakout boards use 5 V power or 5 V logic and may need level shifting.
External amplifier or radio module current draw may exceed what should be sourced from board headers.
Analog audio circuits may need careful grounding to avoid noise.
timing: Sampling jitter can reduce audio quality.
Display updates and serial logging may interfere with audio timing if not scheduled carefully.
Packet retransmission or buffering can add latency.
memory: Audio buffers and recorded voice snippets can consume memory quickly.
Advanced compression or AI features may not fit without careful sizing.
Debug logging buffers may compete with audio buffers.
privacy_security: Voice data may contain personal information.
Wireless transmission should be treated as observable in a lab environment unless encryption is explicitly implemented.
Stored voice snippets should be cleared or documented.
advanced_feature_risks: Audio compression can become a separate signal-processing project.
Edge AI features may require model conversion, memory analysis, and performance testing.
Battery and enclosure work can distract from the embedded software learning goals.

human_approval_required: Approve whether the target scope is local audio trainer, two-device walkie-talkie, or advanced digital voice communicator.
Approve the communication module or technology to use.
Approve whether real-time audio or recorded snippets are acceptable.
Approve the available microphone, speaker, amplifier, and display components.
Approve any module that is not clearly 3.3 V-compatible before wiring it to the FRDM-MCXA153.

handoff_to_requirements_agent.readiness_notes: Proceed with requirements for a staged two-device short-range digital walkie-talkie, but define fallback requirements for local audio capture/playback if the wireless link or audio streaming proves too demanding.
critical_missing_information: Available audio input and output components
Real-time streaming versus voice snippet requirement
